text:
Now, let’s look
behind the interface
My contribution: backend architecture and engineering
I built the services that validate requests, protect data, run background work and support real-time chat.

After my teammates have shown you the product and their parts, I will take you behind the interface and explain the backend. I was responsible for the server-side architecture and implementation. I will show how the backend validates requests, controls permissions, stores data, processes background jobs and powers real-time chat.
Current counts taken from the submitted repository.
Authentication, offers, applications, chat and administration
Identity, recruitment, communication and operational state
Every database change has an ordered history
372 test functions cover security and business workflows
Runtime: API, worker, AI dispatcher, Redis, web client and reverse proxy

Use the numbers as evidence of scope. The important distinction is 163 normal HTTP endpoints plus two WebSocket endpoints, which gives 165 application routes in total. Mention that FastAPI documentation routes are not included.
The API changes its data and permissions according to the authenticated role.
Profiles and CVs, offer discovery, applications, recommendations, interview progress and chat
Offer management, candidate review, hiring stages, feedback, invitations and recruiter chat
User approvals, companies, support, institutions, missions, subscriptions and audit activity
Validate requests, enforce access rules, store durable state and coordinate external services.

Start with the product rather than the technology. Explain who uses the platform and then define your own backend responsibility. Emphasize that the frontend requests an action while the backend decides whether it is valid and permitted.
FastAPI handles immediate requests, durable jobs and live communication differently.
PostgreSQL owns durable state. Redis coordinates temporary work and delivery between processes.

Explain each path separately. Normal requests finish quickly and commit durable state. Long AI or email tasks become outbox jobs before workers process them. WebSockets use short-lived tickets, store messages in PostgreSQL and use Redis for presence and cross-process delivery.
Each layer answers a different question, which keeps large features easier to change and test.
User, session, company context and shared guards
Permissions, workflow transitions and domain rules
AI, email and durable scheduled work
Changing an application stage loads context, checks the transition, locks the row, writes the update and queues notifications in one transaction.

Walk through the five layers from top to bottom. Then use the application-stage example. Routers coordinate the call, services make the business decision, and database constraints remain the final safety net.
Every dependency solves a specific backend problem and adds an operational responsibility.
Async endpoints, validation, dependency injection and OpenAPI
Careful async boundaries and dependency design
Transactions and relational integrity fit recruitment workflows
AI and email leave the request path without losing work
Private CV and image objects stay outside the database
The architecture gained reliability, but deployment and failure handling became part of the backend job.
Avoid listing technologies without reasons. For each row, say what problem it solves and what responsibility it introduces. This shows engineering judgment rather than simply naming a stack.
The same boundary protects all sensitive HTTP endpoints.

Parse body, query
and path data
Approved Origin plus matching CSRF cookie and X-CSRF-Token header.
Expected errors stay explicit. Unexpected failures return a safe message and traceable error ID.

Use a real endpoint during the explanation. The request does not jump directly from the router to the database. Validation, authentication and authorization happen before business logic. Mention CSRF protection for cookie-based mutations and safe error responses.
One application links the candidate, offer, CV snapshot, workflow history, AI screening and interviews.

status  /  stage_version
AI status, score and report
interview schedule and notes
No duplicate application  /  valid status  /  AI score from 0 to 100  /  CV must belong to the candidate

Center the explanation on the Application model. It preserves the state of one candidate applying to one offer. Explain the relationships and then the database guarantees, especially the unique candidate-offer pair and CV ownership constraint.
Two users or workers can act at the same time, so correctness cannot depend on request order.
Example: two recruiters change the same application
SKIP LOCKED lets workers claim different rows
Describe the race condition first. Then walk through the lock, version check and atomic commit. Explain that constraints and idempotency still protect the system if the same command arrives twice.
Session authority changes with account state
A valid token identifies a session, while current database state decides what that session may still do.
JWT contains session_id and auth_version. Redis rejects revoked sessions quickly. PostgreSQL remains the durable source of truth.
Short-lived challenges are consumed atomically to prevent replay.

Explain why token validity alone is insufficient. A user may become inactive, lose a role or change a password after the token was created. auth_version and session revocation remove old authority. Mention that two-factor challenges are single use.
Every protected action combines a role capability with ownership or tenant boundaries.
Role grants application review and chat
Application and offer belong to the recruiter tenant
Otherwise the API returns a safe 403 or 404 response
Candidates access only their own profile, CV, applications, recommendation analysis and allowed conversations.
Foreign resources never reveal private existence.
Use the equation on the slide. A recruiter role may permit application review, but the resource must also belong to the same company. For candidates, ownership provides the main scope boundary.
The backend controls every stage change and keeps an auditable recruitment history.
Before commit: current stage + requested stage + caller permission + application scope

Walk through the recruitment stages. The service never accepts an arbitrary new status. It checks the current stage, requested transition, caller permission and application scope before committing the update and its related history.
AI calls can be slow or unavailable, so the user request only records durable work.
Pending work remains in PostgreSQL after an API or worker restart.
Transient provider failures use bounded retry instead of losing the request.
Leases, claim state and idempotency keep one logical result.

Explain why calling the AI provider directly inside the HTTP request would be fragile. The database first records the job. A dispatcher and worker can then retry safely, while the user checks job status later.
Business data commits first. Email delivery retries independently without sending duplicates.
Fernet encryption protects queued recipient data and message payloads
Retry delay grows from 30 seconds up to a 60-minute limit
A dedupe key and provider idempotency key protect the final effect

Describe a failure after the application stage changes but before the email provider responds. The domain change stays committed, and the email row remains available for retry. Encryption protects queued data, while dedupe and provider idempotency prevent duplicate messages.
The backend supports recruitment chat and private chat between accepted friends.
Candidate and recruiter communication for one authorized application. Current workflow stage can enable or disable access.
Private candidate-to-candidate messaging. Both users must be active candidates with an accepted friendship.
Shared security: single-use socket ticket, session checks, rate limits, PostgreSQL history and Redis fan-out

Clarify that there are two WebSocket endpoint types, not necessarily two permanent connections for every user. The recruitment socket is scoped to an application. The friend socket is scoped to an accepted friendship. Both use short-lived single-use tickets and store durable history in PostgreSQL.
CVs and identity data require stronger controls than public offers and company information.

Explain that private storage credentials remain on the backend. A file never becomes public merely because its URL exists. For account deletion, explain the export, reauthentication, cancellation window and final removal or anonymization of personal data.
Only the reverse proxy accepts public traffic. Data stores and workers remain on private networks.

TLS, HSTS, routing
and WAF rules
Structured logs with traceable error IDs

Describe the public boundary first. Nginx handles TLS and routes traffic to private services. PostgreSQL, Redis and workers do not expose public ports. Then explain how health checks, logs, metrics and startup validation support diagnosis.
The repository contains 53 test files and 372 test functions across the main backend risks.
WebSockets, history, read events and presence
AI jobs, uploads, health and deployment readiness
If the demo fails, the tests still tell the story.

Do not claim that test count alone proves quality. Name the risks covered by the suite. For the live demo, follow one connected workflow so the staff can see identity, permissions, transactions, workers and WebSockets in context.
What I learned and what comes next
The backend work changed how I think about authority, data integrity and failure recovery.
A valid token cannot replace role, tenant and ownership checks.
Constraints and transactions protect workflows when application code fails.
Outboxes and workers keep AI and email work through restarts.
Load and stress tests for chat and application updates
Distributed tracing across API, dispatcher and workers
Clearer job retry and failure dashboards
The backend survived. The cat is still investigating.

Finish with the three lessons rather than repeating the technology list. Mention the next improvements honestly. Invite questions about any layer of the backend, and be ready to open the code or demonstrate one workflow.
